title: Account Takeover Fraud: How to Protect Your Money in 2026
excerpt: Learn the warning signs of account takeover fraud, the steps that protect your bank accounts, and what to do immediately if a criminal gets access.
content:
Account takeover fraud happens when a criminal gets into one of your financial accounts and uses it as if they were you. It can start with a stolen password, a convincing phishing message, a data breach, or even a hijacked phone number. Once inside, the fraudster may change your contact details, move money, open credit, or lock you out before you notice.

The good news is that a few practical habits dramatically reduce the risk. This guide explains the warning signs of account takeover fraud, how to secure your bank and payment accounts, and what to do if access has already been compromised. For broader protection, also read our guides on [how to freeze your credit](/blog/how-to-freeze-your-credit) and [how to spot phishing scams](/blog/how-to-spot-phishing-scams-protect-your-money).

## What is account takeover fraud?

Account takeover fraud is unauthorized access to an account that already belongs to you. The account might be a checking account, credit card, investment account, email inbox, payment app, mobile phone account, or online shopping account.

Unlike a thief who simply uses a stolen card number for one purchase, an account takeover criminal tries to take control. They may reset your password, replace your email address or phone number, add a new transfer recipient, and use your trusted account to make their activity look legitimate.

Your email is especially important. If someone controls your email inbox, they can often reset passwords for many other accounts. Treat it as the master key to your digital financial life.

## How criminals take over accounts

Most account takeovers do not begin with a sophisticated hack. They usually begin with information that has already been exposed or with a moment of pressure that causes someone to act quickly.

### Reused or leaked passwords

When you reuse the same password across multiple sites, one breach can create a chain reaction. Criminals test leaked email and password combinations on bank, shopping, and payment sites. This is often called credential stuffing.

### Phishing messages

A fake bank alert can look convincing on a phone. It may say there is suspicious activity and ask you to click a link or provide a one-time code. The goal is to capture your login details or get you to approve a real login attempt.

### SIM swap fraud

In a SIM swap, a criminal persuades a mobile carrier to move your phone number to a device they control. They may then receive texted security codes and reset account passwords. Learn more in our guide to the [SIM swap scam](/blog/sim-swap-scam-how-to-protect-bank-accounts).

### Malware and fake apps

Malicious software can capture passwords, read notifications, or redirect you to a fake login page. Downloading financial apps only from official app stores and keeping devices updated lowers this risk.

### Social engineering

Fraudsters sometimes call while pretending to be a bank employee, delivery company, or government agency. They use urgency to make you reveal a code or approve a login. A real bank will not ask you to share a one-time verification code that you did not request.

## Warning signs of account takeover fraud

Fast detection limits damage. Watch for these signs, even if you have not yet spotted a missing dollar.

- A password reset email or security code you did not request
- A notification that your email address, phone number, or mailing address changed
- New payees, linked bank accounts, cards, or devices on an account
- A transfer, cash withdrawal, purchase, or payment-app transaction you do not recognize
- Your mobile phone suddenly loses service without an obvious reason
- You are locked out after your password suddenly stops working
- Credit inquiries, accounts, or statements that you did not open

Do not dismiss one of these as a glitch. Open the official app or type the institution's website yourself instead of using a link in a message.

## How to prevent account takeover fraud

No single setting makes you invulnerable, but a layered approach makes you much harder to target.

### Use a unique password for every financial account

Each important account needs its own long, unique password. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so you do not need to memorize dozens of them.

Start with email, banking, credit cards, brokerage accounts, payment apps, and your mobile carrier. If you discover that you have reused a password, change it everywhere it appears, beginning with the accounts that can move money.

### Turn on multi-factor authentication

Multi-factor authentication adds another check beyond your password. An authenticator app or security key is generally stronger than a text message because a SIM swap can intercept text codes.

If a bank only offers text codes, use them anyway. They are still safer than using a password alone. You can also protect your number with a carrier account PIN.

### Secure your email inbox first

Use a unique password and multi-factor authentication on your primary email account. Review its recovery email address, phone number, and active sessions. Remove anything you do not recognize.

Create a habit of reviewing email forwarding rules too. Criminals sometimes add a hidden forwarding rule so they can watch for bank notices after an account is compromised.

### Enable transaction and login alerts

Set alerts for logins, password changes, transfers, purchases, low balances, and new payees. Choose push notifications or email alerts where available.

Alerts are not just for budgeting. They shorten the time between fraud and discovery. That is valuable because banks and payment services can act faster when you report unauthorized activity promptly.

### Add a PIN to your mobile-carrier account

Ask your carrier about a port-out lock, number lock, or account PIN. Names vary, but the goal is the same: make it harder for someone to transfer your phone number without extra verification.

Never share a carrier or bank verification code with a caller. If the request is legitimate, hang up and call the number on your statement or the back of your card.

### Be skeptical of urgent messages

Fraud messages often demand immediate action. They may claim your account will be closed, a payment is pending, or a fraud investigator needs a code right now. Slow down. Urgency is a tactic, not proof.

Check the sender carefully, but do not rely on the display name alone. Fake emails and texts can look similar to real ones. Use the official app or a bookmarked website to verify the issue.

### Review accounts on a schedule

Check your bank and credit card activity at least weekly. A quick review helps you recognize unfamiliar transactions while details are still fresh. A budget tracker such as Pennywise can also make unusual spending easier to notice because you see your normal patterns in one place.

Review your credit reports regularly as well. A [fraud alert or credit freeze](/blog/fraud-alert-vs-credit-freeze) can help if you are concerned that someone may try to open new credit in your name.

## What to do if you think an account has been taken over

Act quickly, but do not panic. Start with the account that controls your password resets, usually email.

### 1. Contact the institution through an official channel

Call the phone number on the back of your card, on your statement, or inside the official app. Tell the fraud department that you suspect an account takeover. Ask them to secure the account, stop pending transfers if possible, and review recent changes.

Do not use a phone number in a suspicious text or email.

### 2. Change credentials from a trusted device

Use a device you trust to change the password and turn on multi-factor authentication. Sign out of other sessions if the service offers that option. Update your email password next if it could be connected to the compromise.

If you think your device may be infected, update it, run a reputable security scan, and avoid entering new passwords until you are confident it is clean.

### 3. Check contact details and recovery settings

Look for unfamiliar email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses, backup codes, linked accounts, forwarding rules, or authorized devices. Remove unauthorized changes and document what you find.

### 4. Review transactions and dispute unauthorized activity

Review recent activity carefully. Save screenshots, confirmation numbers, and copies of messages. Ask the institution how to dispute each transaction and follow its deadlines.

### 5. Contact your mobile carrier if service changed

If your phone unexpectedly loses service or you suspect a SIM swap, contact the carrier immediately from another phone. Ask whether the number was transferred and request account protections.

### 6. Protect your credit if identity theft is possible

If the incident involves personal information, consider placing a fraud alert or freezing your credit with the major credit bureaus. The Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov can help you create a recovery plan and keep records organized.

## Bank account takeover versus credit card fraud

Both are serious, but they require different attention. Credit card fraud often appears as unauthorized purchases on a card. Bank account takeover can be more urgent because it may involve direct access to deposits, bill payments, or transfers.

Report either type quickly. For bank accounts, ask specifically about recent transfers, new external accounts, wire instructions, and changes to your online-banking profile. For credit cards, ask for a replacement card and confirm which charges are being disputed.

## Common mistakes that increase risk

### Reusing a password after a breach

Changing one account is not enough if the same password protects several accounts. Replace it everywhere it was used.

### Approving a login you did not start

A prompt on your phone may be a real security check for a criminal who already knows your password. Deny it if you did not initiate it, then change the password.

### Waiting to see whether a strange alert matters

A surprise verification code, address-change notice, or service outage can be an early warning. Verify it immediately through official channels.

### Sharing one-time codes

One-time codes are meant for you, not for a caller, texter, or email sender. Anyone asking for one is trying to get around a security control.

## A simple 15-minute account security checkup

Use this checklist today:

1. Change any reused password on email and financial accounts.
2. Turn on multi-factor authentication wherever it is available.
3. Add login and transaction alerts to bank and payment accounts.
4. Add a PIN or port-out lock with your mobile carrier.
5. Review recovery settings, linked devices, and forwarding rules on your email account.
6. Check recent bank, credit card, and payment-app activity.
7. Freeze your credit if you have a specific reason to suspect identity theft.

You do not need to do everything perfectly in one sitting. Securing the accounts that control your money and email first gives you the biggest immediate improvement.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is account takeover fraud in simple terms?

It is when someone gains unauthorized access to an existing account and uses it as if they were you. They may change settings, move money, or use the account to reach other accounts.

### Can a bank refund account takeover fraud?

It depends on the facts, the type of transaction, and how quickly you report it. Contact the bank's fraud department immediately and follow its dispute process.

### Is multi-factor authentication enough to stop account takeover?

It is one of the strongest protections, but it works best with unique passwords, account alerts, a secured email inbox, and careful handling of verification codes.

### What should I do if I receive a code I did not request?

Do not share or approve it. Open the official app or website, check your account activity, and change your password if you suspect someone has tried to sign in.

### Can a SIM swap lead to bank account takeover?

Yes. If a criminal controls your phone number, they may receive texted security codes. Use an authenticator app where possible and add extra security with your mobile carrier.

## The bottom line

Account takeover fraud is unsettling because it can move quickly, but prevention is practical. Use unique passwords, protect your email, turn on multi-factor authentication, add alerts, and treat unexpected codes or account changes as urgent signals to verify.

If you suspect a takeover, contact the institution through an official channel right away, secure your email and passwords, and document what happened. Fast action can limit the damage and help you regain control.
